ap_statistics-m01.stem: A random sample of $240$ employees is selected from a large company, and each is assigned at random to work a flexible schedule or to keep the regular schedule. After the study period, the mean job satisfaction score is higher in the group that used the flexible schedule, and the difference is statistically significant. Which conclusion is justified by the design of this study?

options.text: The result does not show that the flexible schedule caused the higher mean job satisfaction score and cannot be generalized to all employees
options.why: Refuses both conclusions, but random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion, but random selection allows generalizing.

options.text: The flexible schedule caused the higher mean job satisfaction score, but the result cannot be generalized beyond the employees in the study
options.why: Claims cause and refuses to generalize even though the sample was randomly selected.

options.text: The result can be generalized to all employees, but it does not show that the flexible schedule caused the higher mean job satisfaction score
options.why: Refuses to conclude cause even though the groups were randomly assigned and generalizes.

options.text: The flexible schedule caused the higher mean job satisfaction score, and the result can be generalized to all employees
options.why: Random assignment supports a cause-and-effect conclusion and random selection supports generalizing.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Decide which conclusions a study design justifies
student_thinking: Check whether treatments were assigned at random, which decides whether a cause-and-effect conclusion is justified
Check whether participants were randomly selected, which decides whether results can be generalized to the population

key_conditions.condition: random assignment allows a causal conclusion and random selection allows generalization
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states how participants were selected and how they were assigned to groups

misconceptions.description: refuses a conclusion that the design justifies

verification.independent_path: a truth table over the two design features is enumerated, exactly one of the four claims is allowed, and the sentences are generated from the same table

ap_statistics-m01.stem: A random sample of $150$ adults is selected from a mid-sized city, and each is assigned at random to follow the exercise plan or to not follow it. After the study period, the mean weight loss is higher in the group that used the exercise plan, and the difference is statistically significant. Which conclusion is justified by the design of this study?

options.text: The result can be generalized to all adults, but it does not show that the exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss
options.why: Refuses to conclude cause even though the groups were randomly assigned and generalizes.

options.text: The exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss, and the result can be generalized to all adults
options.why: Random assignment supports a cause-and-effect conclusion and random selection supports generalizing.

options.text: The result does not show that the exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss and cannot be generalized to all adults
options.why: Refuses both conclusions, but random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion, but random selection allows generalizing.

options.text: The exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss, but the result cannot be generalized beyond the adults in the study
options.why: Claims cause and refuses to generalize even though the sample was randomly selected.

ap_statistics-m02.stem: A researcher wants to study how far employees of a large company commute to work. Which of the following is a valid investigative question that requires a statistical investigation?

options.text: How many employees does the company have at its headquarters?
options.why: Asks for a single count that can be looked up, so no variability in data is anticipated and no statistical investigation is needed.

options.text: Do employees of the company who work downtown commute shorter distances than employees who work at other offices?
options.why: Anticipates variability among the individuals, names the population and can be answered by collecting and analyzing data.

options.text: Should the company allow its employees to work from home?
options.why: Asks for an opinion or a value judgment that data collection and analysis cannot settle.

options.text: How many miles did Mr. Gomez drive to work yesterday?
options.why: Asks about one individual, so there is no population and no variability to investigate.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Recognize a valid investigative question that requires a statistical investigation
student_thinking: Check whether the question anticipates variability among individuals rather than asking for one fixed value
Check that the question names a population and can be answered by collecting and analyzing data, not by opinion

key_conditions.condition: a valid investigative question anticipates variability, refers to a population and can be answered with data
key_conditions.evidence: three options each lack exactly one of these three properties

misconceptions.description: asks for a count or fact that can be looked up

verification.independent_path: each option is generated from a table of three properties (variability, population, answerable with data) and exactly one option has all three

options.text: How many employees does the company have at its headquarters?

options.text: What proportion of the company's employees commute more than twenty miles one way?

ap_statistics-m03.stem: A random sample of $300$ households in a town was surveyed, and the variables in the table shown were recorded for each individual. Which of the following investigative questions can be answered using these data?

stimulus.description: Variables recorded for each of 300 households in a town.

options.text: What was the monthly electric bill for each of the households?
options.why: Asks for a listing of individual values rather than a question about a population that can be answered by summarizing and analyzing the data.

options.text: Is there an association between the number of residents in a household and its monthly electric bill?
options.why: Uses only variables that were recorded and asks about a relationship that the recorded data can address.

options.text: Do households with a higher annual income have a larger monthly electric bill?
options.why: Needs a variable that was not recorded, so the data cannot answer it.

options.text: Would adding another resident to a household cause its monthly electric bill to increase?
options.why: A cause-and-effect question needs data from a randomized experiment, but these data were only recorded, not assigned.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Decide which investigative question the collected data can answer
student_thinking: Match the variables named in each question to the variables in the table
Reject questions that need uncollected variables, need random assignment for a cause-and-effect claim, or ask for individual values

key_conditions.condition: an investigative question must be answerable with the collected variables and the study design
key_conditions.evidence: the table lists every variable that was recorded and the stem says the data come from a survey

misconceptions.description: needs a variable that was not recorded
asks a cause-and-effect question of survey data
asks for a list of individual values

verification.independent_path: the variable names in each option are matched mechanically against the table and exactly one option uses only recorded variables and an association question

ap_statistics-m03.stem: A random sample of $180$ adult members of a gym was surveyed, and the variables in the table shown were recorded for each individual. Which of the following investigative questions can be answered using these data?

stimulus.description: Variables recorded for each of 180 adult members of a gym.

options.text: Do members with a higher resting heart rate visit the gym more often?
options.why: Needs a variable that was not recorded, so the data cannot answer it.

options.text: Is there an association between a gym member's years of membership and visits last month?
options.why: Uses only variables that were recorded and asks about a relationship that the recorded data can address.

options.text: Would switching to a premium membership cause a member to visit the gym more often?
options.why: A cause-and-effect question needs data from a randomized experiment, but these data were only recorded, not assigned.

options.text: What was the number of visits last month for each of the members?
options.why: Asks for a listing of individual values rather than a question about a population that can be answered by summarizing and analyzing the data.

ap_statistics-m04.stem: The company wants a sample of $50$ employees from a list of $800$ in which every group of $50$ employees is equally likely to be chosen. The plan is to number the employees from $1$ to $800$ and use a random number generator to choose $50$ different numbers. Which of the following best describes this sampling method?

options.text: A convenience sample
options.why: Chooses whoever is easy to reach, which is likely to be biased and does not use random selection.

options.text: A simple random sample
options.why: This method matches the goal: number the employees from $1$ to $800$ and use a random number generator to choose $50$ different numbers.

options.text: A stratified random sample
options.why: Does not guarantee that each subgroup is represented in proportion; only random selection within each subgroup guarantees it.

options.text: A cluster sample
options.why: Selects whole groups at random and surveys every member, which does not match a goal of spreading the sample across the list.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Justify a sampling method that fits a stated goal
student_thinking: Identify the goal stated in the scenario, such as representation of subgroups, cost of reaching whole groups or equal chance for every group of the chosen size
Match that goal and the described plan to the one sampling method that has this property

key_conditions.condition: each sampling method has a defining property that matches one goal
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states both the goal and the selection plan

misconceptions.description: treats a convenience sample as random

verification.independent_path: a table of methods and defining properties is used and exactly one method has the property required by the stated goal

ap_statistics-m04.stem: Traveling to many apartment buildings is too costly, so the manager wants to survey all residents in only a few buildings. The plan is to randomly select $5$ of the $40$ apartment buildings and survey every resident in the selected buildings. Which of the following best describes this sampling method?

options.text: A stratified random sample
options.why: Does not guarantee that each subgroup is represented in proportion; only random selection within each subgroup guarantees it.

options.text: A cluster sample
options.why: This method matches the goal: randomly select $5$ of the $40$ apartment buildings and survey every resident in the selected buildings.

options.text: A simple random sample
options.why: Gives every group of the chosen size the same chance, but does not guarantee representation of each subgroup.

options.text: A convenience sample
options.why: Chooses whoever is easy to reach, which is likely to be biased and does not use random selection.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics

student_thinking: Identify the goal stated in the scenario, such as representation of subgroups, cost of reaching whole groups or equal chance for every group of the chosen size
Match that goal and the described plan to the one sampling method that has this property

key_conditions.condition: each sampling method has a defining property that matches one goal
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states both the goal and the selection plan

ap_statistics-m05.stem: The boxplots shown display delivery times, in minutes, for Store A and Store B. The gridlines mark equal steps on the horizontal axis. Which of the following statements is correct?

stimulus.description: Side-by-side boxplots of delivery times, in minutes

options.text: The third quartile of Store A is greater than the third quartile of Store B
options.why: The third quartile of Store A is $72$ and that of Store B is $79$ (the right edge of each box), so this comparison is reversed.

options.text: The maximum of Store A is greater than the maximum of Store B
options.why: The maximum of Store A is $77$ and that of Store B is $92$ (the right end of each upper whisker), so this comparison is reversed.

options.text: The interquartile range of Store A is greater than the interquartile range of Store B
options.why: The interquartile range of Store A is $16$ and that of Store B is $26$ (the lengths of the boxes), so this comparison is reversed.

options.text: The median of Store A is greater than the median of Store B
options.why: This comparison is true for the plotted five-number summaries.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Compare two distributions displayed in boxplots
student_thinking: Read the median, the quartiles and the whisker ends for each group from the boxplot
Evaluate each statement about center, spread or extremes and keep the one that matches the plotted values

key_conditions.condition: a boxplot shows the minimum, the quartiles, the median and the maximum
key_conditions.evidence: the boxplots show the five-number summaries of both groups with no outliers, and every compared statistic differs by at least six units

verification.independent_path: each statement is evaluated against the plotted five-number summaries, every compared statistic is required to differ by at least six units so the difference is visible, and exactly one of the four chosen statements is true

ap_statistics-m06.stem: A researcher plans to collect data from a random sample of customers of a coffee shop to answer the following investigative question: "Among customers of a coffee shop, is there a relationship between the number of minutes spent in the shop and the amount spent, in dollars, on a visit?" Which of the following best describes what this question asks about?

options.text: A question about the association between two categorical variables
options.why: The question names two quantitative variables, not two categorical variables.

options.text: A question that compares a quantitative variable between two groups
options.why: The question names two quantitative variables, not a quantitative variable and a categorical variable that defines two groups.

options.text: A question about the proportion of individuals in one category of a categorical variable
options.why: The question names two quantitative variables, not one categorical variable.

options.text: A question about the relationship between two quantitative variables
options.why: The question names two quantitative variables, which is the structure this option describes.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Recognize what an investigative question asks about: one distribution, a comparison of groups or an association
student_thinking: List the variables that the question names and decide whether each is quantitative or categorical
Match the number and types of variables, and whether groups are compared, to the one option with the same structure

key_conditions.condition: a valid investigative question names the variables it asks about, so its structure follows from the variables named
key_conditions.evidence: the question is stated in the stem and every option describes a different variable structure

misconceptions.description: names one variable when the question names two or the reverse
mixes up quantitative and categorical variables
mixes up comparing two groups with a relationship between two variables

verification.independent_path: the five question structures are generated from a table of (quantitative count, categorical count, groups compared) and exactly one row matches the question

ap_statistics-m06.stem: A researcher plans to collect data from a random sample of adult members of a fitness center to answer the following investigative question: "Among adult members of a fitness center, is there a relationship between the number of years as a member and the number of visits to the center in a month?" Which of the following best describes what this question asks about?

options.text: A question that compares a quantitative variable between two groups
options.why: The question names two quantitative variables, not a quantitative variable and a categorical variable that defines two groups.

options.text: A question about the relationship between two quantitative variables
options.why: The question names two quantitative variables, which is the structure this option describes.

options.text: A question about the distribution of one quantitative variable
options.why: The question names two quantitative variables, not one quantitative variable.

options.text: A question about the proportion of individuals in one category of a categorical variable
options.why: The question names two quantitative variables, not one categorical variable.

ap_statistics-m07.stem: The table shown summarizes the responses of $156$ patients. One patient is selected at random. Given that the patient improved, what is the probability that the patient was treated at the North clinic? Round to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Two-way table of clinic and response

options.why: Reports the overall proportion in the row, ignoring the given information.
Divides by the row total instead of the column total, which reverses the condition.
Given the column, the total is $87$ and $45$ of them are in the row: $45/87 \approx 0.517$.
Divides by the grand total, which gives the probability of both events instead of the conditional probability.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Compute a conditional probability from a two-way table
student_thinking: Restrict attention to the group named by the given condition (one column)
Divide the count of the event within that group by the group total, not by the grand total or the row total

key_conditions.condition: P(A given B) divides the joint count by the total for B
key_conditions.evidence: the table gives all counts and the stem names the given condition

verification.independent_path: every respondent is expanded into an individual record and the conditional proportion is found by enumeration, independent of the cell-count ratio

ap_statistics-m07.stem: The table shown summarizes the responses of $154$ patients. One patient is selected at random. Given that the patient did not improve, what is the probability that the patient was treated at the North clinic? Round to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Two-way table of clinic and response

options.why: Divides by the row total instead of the column total, which reverses the condition.
Reports the overall proportion in the row, ignoring the given information.
Given the column, the total is $95$ and $46$ of them are in the row: $46/95 \approx 0.484$.
Divides by the grand total, which gives the probability of both events instead of the conditional probability.

ap_statistics-m08.stem: At an email filter, each email comes from Inbox Work or Inbox Personal, as shown in the tree diagram. One email is selected at random and is flagged. What is the probability that the email is a work email? Round to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Probability tree for Inbox and outcome

options.why: $P(\text{Work}\mid \text{flagged}) = 0.0600/0.0800 \approx 0.750$: the branch for Work then flagged, divided by the total probability of flagged.
Reports the overall probability of being flagged, not the probability of Work given that.
Reports the probability of being flagged given Work, which reverses the conditional probability asked for.
Reports the probability of Work and flagged together, without dividing by the probability of being flagged.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Reverse a conditional probability using a probability tree
student_thinking: Compute the probability of each path ending in the given outcome
Divide the path through the named source by the total probability of the outcome

key_conditions.condition: P(source given outcome) = P(source and outcome) / P(outcome)
key_conditions.evidence: the tree gives the source probabilities and the conditional outcome probabilities on each branch

verification.independent_path: a population of 100000 items is built from the tree with integer counts per path and the conditional proportion is computed from the counts

ap_statistics-m08.stem: At an electronics assembler, each part comes from Supplier A or Supplier B, as shown in the tree diagram. One part is selected at random and is faulty. What is the probability that the part came from Supplier A? Round to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Probability tree for Supplier and outcome

options.why: Reports the probability of A before the faulty information is used.
Reports the overall probability of being faulty, not the probability of A given that.
$P(\text{A}\mid \text{faulty}) = 0.0600/0.0720 \approx 0.833$: the branch for A then faulty, divided by the total probability of faulty.
Reports the probability of being faulty given A, which reverses the conditional probability asked for.

blueprint.concept: Reverse a conditional probability using a probability tree
student_thinking: Compute the probability of each path ending in the given outcome
Divide the path through the named source by the total probability of the outcome

key_conditions.evidence: the tree gives the source probabilities and the conditional outcome probabilities on each branch

verification.independent_path: a population of 100000 items is built from the tree with integer counts per path and the conditional proportion is computed from the counts

ap_statistics-m09.stem: The repair costs, in dollars, for repairs at a garage are skewed to the right with mean $60$ and standard deviation $30$. The dotplot shown displays the means of $40$ simulated random samples of $100$ values from this population. Which describes the sampling distribution of the sample mean for samples of size $100$?

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $60$ and standard deviation $30$
options.why: Keeps the population standard deviation instead of dividing it by the square root of the sample size.

options.text: Skewed to the right like the population, with mean $60$ and standard deviation $3$
options.why: Believes the sampling distribution keeps the shape of the skewed population even with a large sample size.

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $60$ and standard deviation $0.3$
options.why: Divides the population standard deviation by $n$ instead of by the square root of $n$.

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $60$ and standard deviation $3$
options.why: The mean of the sampling distribution is $\mu=60$ and its standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}=30/\sqrt{100}=3$; with $100$ observations the Central Limit Theorem makes it approximately normal.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Describe the sampling distribution of a sample mean using the Central Limit Theorem
student_thinking: Find the mean and the standard deviation of the sampling distribution from the population values and the sample size
Decide the shape of the sampling distribution from the sample size even though the population is skewed

key_conditions.condition: the sampling distribution of the mean has mean mu, standard deviation sigma over root n and is approximately normal for large n
key_conditions.evidence: the sample size is large (at least 30) and the population standard deviation is given

verification.independent_path: 4000 simulated samples from a gamma population with the same mean and standard deviation reproduce the stated mean and standard deviation, and the plotted means are checked against them

ap_statistics-m09.stem: The lengths of phone calls, in minutes, for calls to a help line are skewed to the right with mean $60$ and standard deviation $30$. The dotplot shown displays the means of $40$ simulated random samples of $64$ values from this population. Which describes the sampling distribution of the sample mean for samples of size $64$?

options.text: Skewed to the right like the population, with mean $60$ and standard deviation $3.75$
options.why: Believes the sampling distribution keeps the shape of the skewed population even with a large sample size.

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $60$ and standard deviation $0.469$
options.why: Divides the population standard deviation by $n$ instead of by the square root of $n$.

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $60$ and standard deviation $30$
options.why: Keeps the population standard deviation instead of dividing it by the square root of the sample size.

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $60$ and standard deviation $3.75$
options.why: The mean of the sampling distribution is $\mu=60$ and its standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}=30/\sqrt{64}=3.75$; with $64$ observations the Central Limit Theorem makes it approximately normal.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Describe the sampling distribution of a sample mean using the Central Limit Theorem
student_thinking: Find the mean and the standard deviation of the sampling distribution from the population values and the sample size
Decide the shape of the sampling distribution from the sample size even though the population is skewed

key_conditions.condition: the sampling distribution of the mean has mean mu, standard deviation sigma over root n and is approximately normal for large n
key_conditions.evidence: the sample size is large (at least 30) and the population standard deviation is given

verification.independent_path: 4000 simulated samples from a gamma population with the same mean and standard deviation reproduce the stated mean and standard deviation, and the plotted means are checked against them

ap_statistics-m10.stem: A seed company states that $60\%$ of its seeds germinate. A gardener suspects the stated value is not correct. Let $p$ be the proportion of all seeds that germinate. Which of the following pairs of hypotheses should be tested?

options.why: Writes a one-sided alternative although the suspicion only says the claim is not accurate, without a direction. Picks the lower direction.
Writes a one-sided alternative although the suspicion only says the claim is not accurate, without a direction. Picks the upper direction.
Puts the claim of the suspicion in the null hypothesis and an equal sign in the alternative, instead of an equal sign in the null.
The parameter is the proportion of all seeds that germinate; the null hypothesis states the claimed value and the alternative matches the suspicion, which is two-sided.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Choose the null and alternative hypotheses from a scenario
student_thinking: Identify the population parameter and the claimed value that goes in the null hypothesis
Match the direction of the alternative hypothesis to the direction of the suspicion

key_conditions.condition: the null hypothesis states equality with the claimed value and the alternative reflects what is suspected
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states the claim and the direction of the suspicion in words

misconceptions.description: uses an alternative in the wrong direction
writes hypotheses about a sample statistic
swaps the roles of the two hypotheses

verification.independent_path: each option is built from a table of direction, parameter symbol and role of the equality, and only one row matches the scenario's claim and suspicion

ap_statistics-m10.stem: A seed company states that $60\%$ of its seeds germinate. A gardener suspects the true proportion is higher than stated. Let $p$ be the proportion of all seeds that germinate. Which of the following pairs of hypotheses should be tested?

options.why: Writes the hypotheses about a sample statistic, but hypotheses are always about the population parameter.
Puts the claim of the suspicion in the null hypothesis and an equal sign in the alternative, instead of an equal sign in the null.
The parameter is the proportion of all seeds that germinate; the null hypothesis states the claimed value and the alternative matches the suspicion, which is one-sided.
Reverses the direction of the alternative hypothesis relative to the suspicion.

ap_statistics-m12.stem: A teacher wants to know whether a review session changes test scores. Each student's score is recorded on a test before the session and on a similar test after the session, and the difference is found as before minus after. The teacher suspects only that the review session changes the mean score. Let $\mu_d$ be the mean difference (before minus after), in points, for all students. Which of the following pairs of hypotheses should be tested?

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d < 0$
options.why: Writes a one-sided alternative in the lower direction, but the suspicion only says the value is different, without a direction.

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d \ne 0$
options.why: The parameter is the mean difference (before minus after), in points, for all students; the null hypothesis states the claimed value and the alternative matches the suspicion and the order of subtraction in the definition.

options.text: $H_0: \bar{x}_d = 0$ and $H_a: \bar{x}_d \ne 0$
options.why: Writes the hypotheses about a sample mean, but hypotheses are always about the population parameter.

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d > 0$
options.why: Writes a one-sided alternative in the upper direction, but the suspicion only says the value is different, without a direction.

ap_statistics-m13.stem: The scatterplot shown displays $11$ observations of the daily high temperature (in degrees Fahrenheit) and the number of visitors to a park. The point circled in red is removed, and the least-squares line and the correlation coefficient are recomputed. Which statement describes the effect of removing the point?

options.text: The correlation becomes stronger and the slope becomes steeper
options.why: Without the circled point $|r|$ changes from $0.79$ to $0.95$ and the slope magnitude from $1.42$ to $2.54$.

options.text: The correlation becomes stronger and the slope becomes less steep
options.why: Gets the effect on the slope backwards: the circled point was pulling the line flatter, so the slope gets steeper without it.

options.text: The correlation becomes weaker and the slope becomes steeper
options.why: Gets the effect on the correlation backwards: the remaining points lie closer to a line, so the correlation gets stronger.

options.text: The correlation becomes weaker and the slope becomes less steep
options.why: Treats the effects on the correlation and on the slope as opposite to what they are.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Describe how removing an influential point changes the correlation and the slope
student_thinking: Notice that the circled point has an extreme x-value and does not follow the pattern of the other points
Decide how removing it changes the strength of the correlation and the steepness of the least-squares line

key_conditions.condition: a high-leverage point far from the pattern weakens the correlation and changes the slope
key_conditions.evidence: the plot shows the circled point far to the right of the other observations

verification.independent_path: slope and correlation are recomputed with and without the point by closed-form sums and by numpy polyfit and corrcoef, and the changes must exceed fixed thresholds so the options are distinct
